title: Mind-Auditor cannot address the Mind, so the anti-stagnation corrective arm is disconnected
description: mind-auditor detected STAGNANT and synthesised a 30490-char verbatim injection, but delivery to the Mind failed: agent role names do not resolve between sibling subagents on Claude Code. Both mind and olt-mind bounced with No agent named X is reachable; only the raw handle resolved. The watchdog could detect and log but not correct, so every STAGNANT verdict logged a defect nothing acted on until the main thread relayed by hand.

context.workaround: auditor sends payload to main, main relays to the handle
context.impact: corrective arm disconnected without a human relay

title: plan:brainstorm resolves a bare run id against the repo root and creates a capsule-shaped decoy directory there
description: Given a bare run id rather than a path, plan:brainstorm resolved it repo-root-relative and wrote 434 KB of brainstorming.json into a new capsule-shaped directory at the repository root, while the real capsule under .olt/capsules/<id> never received the file. Every sibling command resolves the same bare id correctly, so the mis-resolution is isolated to plan:brainstorm. Evidence: the root directory held exactly one event, plan-brainstormed at 20:35:30.928Z, two minutes AFTER plan:init at 20:33:41 which had correctly created .olt/capsules/booking-contracts-r1 with manifest, state.json, prompt.md and a 925-file runtime pin. plan:init was not the culprit. Two stray capsule-shaped directories appeared in the owner git status as a result.

context.decoy_contents: events.jsonl with a single plan-brainstormed event, plus brainstorming.json 434KB
context.expected: resolve bare run id to .olt/capsules/<id> like sibling commands; never create a capsule-shaped directory at repo root
context.impact: root hygiene breach plus 434KB of planning output written where no command will read it

title: plan:audit and doctor given a bare run id resolve to the decoy and report phantom integrity failures against a healthy capsule
description: Once the decoy directory existed at the repo root, plan:audit and doctor invoked with the same bare run id resolved to the decoy rather than the real capsule and reported INTEGRITY plus 14 phantom issues, while the real capsule was Healthy with zero issues under an explicit --run path. A supervisor acting on that reading nearly ordered a destructive re-init: re-running plan:init would have discarded the verbatim prompt capture, the 925-file runtime pin, the enhanced plan digest, all 9 chained events and the 3-task planning buffer, to repair a directory that was never the capsule.

context.near_miss: supervisor-ordered plan:init re-run refused by the orchestrator on evidence
context.expected: diagnostics must resolve bare run ids identically to lifecycle commands, or refuse a bare id outright rather than silently reporting on a different directory

title: plan:init resolves a bare run id against --repo while plan:brainstorm and doctor resolve it against cwd
description: Two orchestrators independently established the same split: plan:init resolves a bare run id relative to --repo and lands correctly in .olt/capsules/<id>, while plan:brainstorm and doctor resolve the same bare id relative to cwd. The divergence produced capsule-shaped decoy directories at the repository root holding a single orphaned plan-brainstormed event plus a 434-498KB brainstorming.json, and caused diagnostics to report phantom failures against healthy capsules. Standing workaround adopted by the fleet: always pass the full capsule path.

context.expected: one resolution rule for a bare run id across every command, or refuse the bare form outright

title: doctor fails a healthy capsule because the layout manifest does not declare brainstorming.json
description: plan:brainstorm --save writes brainstorming.json (434-498KB) into the capsule root, but the capsule layout manifest does not declare that filename, so doctor reports Healthy: no with LAYOUT_UNDECLARED: capsule holds an undeclared entry: brainstorming.json. The harness flags its own output as contraband. Non-blocking for execution, but any run that legitimately brainstorms reports unhealthy permanently, which degrades doctor as a signal for every supervisor watching that capsule.

context.expected: declare brainstorming.json in the capsule layout manifest, or write it under a declared subdirectory
context.impact: doctor reports Healthy: no forever on any brainstormed capsule; supervisors lose a trustworthy health signal

title: Stagnation telemetry reports actor mind-1 while the live Mind registers as mind_pulse-gen-1
description: Every mind:audit:live injection is emitted with agentId mind-1, but the Mind actually registered and writing to the capsule event stream is mind_pulse-gen-1. The auditor therefore tracks and injects against an actor id that no agent holds. The Mind reports the injection payload was wrong on all four of its assertions simultaneously: actor mind-1 (real actor is mind_pulse-gen-1), idle 180s (mind:wake reported MODE work), pendingBacklogCount 0 (eight candidates decided on the event log), unresolvedDefectCount 0 (three harness defects recorded that same round).

context.expected: derive the actor from the capsule agent registry rather than a fixed literal, and source backlog and defect counts from the same ledgers the run actually writes
context.impact: the auditor watches an actor that does not exist and injects telemetry the Mind can prove false, which trains supervisors to distrust the watchdog

title: A 120s wall clock cannot tell a stalled Mind from one correctly blocked on an authority gate or a host ceiling
description: Most Mind pauses this session were legitimate: waiting on owner authority:decide events for eight candidates, and waiting on host concurrent-subagent slots after the 12-agent ceiling refused two dispatches. The wall-clock detector scores all of these as stagnation and logs a defect each time, so the ledger fills with entries describing correct behaviour and the real signal is diluted.

context.expected: treat an open pulse inside its deadline, an undecided candidate, or a refused dispatch as blocked rather than stagnant
context.impact: 25 stagnation defects logged this session, most of them describing a Mind that was correctly waiting

title: agent:register cannot record a parent that holds its grant in a different capsule, so the Mind-to-orchestrator link is lost
description: orchestrator_driver-compliance registered in driver-compliance-r1 with --parent-agent mind_pulse-gen-1 and was refused: INVALID_STATE, agent mind_pulse-gen-1 holds no grant. The Mind grant lives in the mind-gen-1 capsule, not the lane capsule, so a Tier 1 orchestrator cannot express its real parent and must register with no parent at all. Every per-lane capsule therefore shows an orchestrator with no ancestry, and the 4-tier chain is reconstructible only inside the mind capsule. The orchestrator recorded the refusal and registered without the flag rather than inventing a local parent.

context.error: INVALID_STATE: agent mind_pulse-gen-1 holds no grant
context.expected: allow a parent grant held in a supervising capsule to be referenced, or record the cross-capsule parent as an attributed external ancestor
context.impact: lineage chains break at every capsule boundary; agent:list in a lane capsule cannot say who deployed the orchestrator

title: An agent released in the supervising capsule stays active in the lane capsule it is driving
description: mind-gen-1 at rev 46 records 8 agents, 4 active and 4 released, the released set being orchestrator_scripts-filesize, orchestrator_docs-archival, orchestrator_auth-common and orchestrator_fleet-admin. The same identities are still ACTIVE in their lane capsules: orchestrator_scripts-filesize is active in scripts-filesize-r1 and orchestrator_docs-archival is active in docs-archival-r1. Two lanes that mind:wake still lists as live are therefore being driven, on paper, by orchestrators the Mind has already released. Each capsule keeps an independent agent registry with no cross-capsule reconciliation, so a release is local to the capsule it was issued in and any supervisor reading a lane capsule sees a roster the supervising capsule has already invalidated.

context.expected: propagate agent:release across capsules that registered the same identity, or refuse to register an identity already released by its supervisor
context.impact: rosters disagree between supervisor and lane; stale-lease recovery and agent:list are unreliable across capsule boundaries

title: Two capsules can stage identical task ids for one objective with no retirement marker and no collision guard
description: This occurred twice in one session. money-contracts-r1 (rev 14, no implementers) and money-contracts-r2 (rev 25, five active implementers impl_money-payout/refund/payment/ledger/pricing) both stage the identical five ids and both register the same orchestrator_money-contracts and coordinator_money-contracts identities. scripts-filesize-r1 (rev 14, orchestrator and coordinator active) and scripts-filesize-r2 (rev 12, zero agents) both stage task-split-simulators, task-split-strip-comments and task-extend-file-size-gate. Neither pair carries any retirement marker, so nothing on disk records which capsule is authoritative and nothing prevents both from dispatching implementers against identical write scopes, which would break the disjoint-write-scope invariant outright. A supervisor asked to retire one had already picked the wrong one from recollection.

context.expected: refuse to stage a task id already staged in another live capsule for the same objective, and provide a recorded retirement marker so authority is readable from disk rather than recalled
context.impact: silent path to two capsules dispatching against identical write scopes; no on-disk answer to which capsule is true

title: plan:init rejects absolute run paths while other commands require them, so no single path rule is safe to teach a fleet
description: Three forms behave differently and no command surface documents the split. Absolute path: plan:init hard-rejects it with run_id must be an identifier, not a path, while doctor and mind:audit:live accept it. Bare id: accepted everywhere but resolves against cwd for plan:brainstorm and doctor, producing repo-root decoy directories and silently bypassing the RBAC engine. Repo-relative .olt/capsules/<id>: the only form verified to work across every command. A supervisor issued always absolute as a fleet-wide rule, had to verify all three forms by hand, and reissue the correction to every live lane. The main-thread relay had propagated the same ambiguous full capsule path wording.

context.absolute: rejected by plan:init, accepted by doctor and mind:audit:live
context.bare_id: accepted everywhere, resolves against cwd for plan:brainstorm and doctor, bypasses RBAC
context.expected: accept one canonical form everywhere, or reject the unsupported forms with an error naming the form that works
context.impact: fleet-wide rules issued by supervisors are wrong for some commands; corrections must be re-broadcast mid-run

title: task:check does not load bun-types, so it reports TS2307 on every bun test file and pressures implementers toward @ts-ignore
description: task:check reports TS2307 Cannot find module bun:test or its corresponding type declarations on newly written suites AND identically on tests/unit/money-contracts.test.ts, a pre-existing committed file that is green in the repo toolchain. That control case proves the failure is in task:check rather than in the code under test: it does not load bun-types. The TypeScript arm is therefore unusable as a gate for this repo and hands every implementer a phantom defect on work that is correct. The direct danger is that an implementer trying to clear TS2307 reaches for @ts-ignore or @ts-nocheck, which breaks the zero-suppression invariant the same gate exists to protect. The AST arm is sound and reads 0 any and 0 suppressions.

context.control_case: tests/unit/money-contracts.test.ts, pre-existing, committed, green in repo toolchain
context.expected: resolve bun-types (or the project tsconfig types field) before typechecking, or skip the TS arm when the runtime types are not resolvable and say so
context.impact: every implementer on a bun repo receives a phantom type defect; the plausible fix is a suppression, so the gate actively pressures agents into violating G1

title: scripts/check/file-size.sh is repo-wide, so one over-limit file fails the completion gate of every concurrent lane
description: The gate globs tests/**/*.ts across tracked and untracked files with LIMIT=300 and sits in every lane gate string. Independent orchestrations with strictly disjoint write scopes therefore share a single failure surface: a file written by the booking lane can fail the money lane completion gate and vice versa, and whichever lane seals second inherits the other lane disjointness cannot protect it from. Observed live: booking-request-contracts.test.ts sat at 298 lines, two from failing every concurrent lane. It also uses git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard, so untracked files are checked and nothing hides by staying unstaged.

context.expected: scope a completion gate to the lane write scope, or declare repo-wide gates explicitly so supervisors know sealing order matters
context.impact: cross-run gate coupling between orchestrations that the harness otherwise guarantees are disjoint

title: The stagnation machinery does not merely mislabel an active Mind, it reclaims its open pulse mid-candidate
description: At 20:55:34.156Z mind:audit:live returned STAGNANT, idle 147s, pending_backlog 0, defect_created true. Across that same window the fleet committed +48 capsule revisions: booking-contracts-r1 67 to 73, driver-compliance-r1 24 to 38, money-contracts-r2 27 to 42, scripts-filesize-r2 23 to 34, mind-gen-1 46 to 48. The mind capsule event log settles it: seq 47 is mind-candidate-opened under actor mind_pulse-gen-1, meaning the Mind was performing supervisory work AND the backlog was non-empty at the moment the audit reported backlog 0. seq 48 is mind-pulse-reclaimed under actor watchdog. So the watchdog reclaimed the open pulse of a demonstrably working Mind while it was mid-candidate. This escalates the threshold defect from a reporting fault to a state mutation against live work.

context.expected: never reclaim a pulse whose owner has emitted events inside the idle window, and derive backlog from the capsule candidate state rather than a ledger the run does not write
context.impact: a working Mind loses its pulse mid-candidate; generational rotation can be seized from a live supervisor by a wall-clock timer

title: The stagnation injection ships the skill default mind manifest, redirecting a Mind to repo roots outside the charter it is actually serving
description: The 30490-char verbatim prompt that mind:audit:live builds and the auditor injects declares repo_roots olt/, tests/, docs/ and goals about the olt ecosystem. That is the skill default manifest at ~/.agents/skills/olt/agents/mind.yaml, not the charter this run is pinned to. The active charter is .olt/charter.yaml, digest 7807812893cb81d663200e095c33bbf0fd4000ebed53052948059b75f37b6048, with roots apps/, packages/, tests/, docs/, scripts/. A Mind obeying the injection verbatim would begin mutating olt/, which is outside its charter roots and which its own non-goals explicitly forbid. The Mind caught it and refused. The failure is silent: an authoritative-looking verbatim manifest quietly redirects work into the wrong tree, and verbatim injection is exactly the mechanism agents are told never to edit or second-guess. The same payload also mandates never pause admitted tasks, dispatch immediately, which directly contradicts a host concurrent-subagent ceiling that has already refused dispatches, so obeying it would create more paused-admitted items rather than fewer.

context.conflicting_mandate: never pause admitted tasks, dispatch immediately — contradicts the host 12-subagent ceiling
context.expected: build the injection from the capsule pinned charter rather than the skill default manifest, and refuse to inject a manifest whose digest does not match the capsule pin
context.impact: a compliant Mind is instructed to write outside its charter roots by the very payload it is told to obey verbatim

title: Gate commands run without a shell, so multi-check completion gates are rejected as weak and the sealed graph enforces only the test command
description: plan:compile rejected a four-part completion gate with gates[3].command must perform substantive verification. Root cause read from gate-command-policy.ts: gate commands are parsed to argv and executed WITHOUT a shell, so any && chain is weak by construction, and bash <script> is weak because bash appears in SHELL_EXECUTABLES. The orchestrator had to reduce its sealed gate to the three-file bun test alone. no-suppressions.sh, file-size.sh and typecheck are therefore enforced only by process discipline and human review, NOT by the task graph. The run seals green while three of its four declared quality checks are outside mechanical enforcement, and nothing in the compiled topology records that reduction.

context.cause: argv execution without a shell; bash is in SHELL_EXECUTABLES
context.expected: support a multi-check gate as a declared list rather than a shell chain, or record the reduction in the compiled topology so a reader can see which declared checks the graph actually enforces
context.impact: a sealed run can report green while most of its declared quality gates were never mechanically run

title: run:exec -- bash scripts/check/x.sh is rejected as UNSHIELDED_COMMAND_DEFECT; only the direct ./script form works
description: Same root cause as the gate policy: bash is in SHELL_EXECUTABLES, so run:exec -- bash scripts/check/no-suppressions.sh is refused as [UNSHIELDED_COMMAND_DEFECT]. The working form is run:exec -- ./scripts/check/no-suppressions.sh. This matters fleet-wide because briefing templates, charter stability blocks and supervisor instructions across this run all use the bash <script> form, so every lane that copies them fails the same way and burns a cycle discovering it. The repo charter stability entries themselves are written as bash scripts/check/file-size.sh.

context.expected: accept the bash <script> form for a repo-local script, or emit an error naming the working form
context.impact: every briefing template and charter stability entry using bash <script> fails on first use across every lane

title: task:check writes command-executed events under actor mechanic-validator, a role the skill retired, inviting false role-violation reports
description: driver-compliance-r1 shows command-executed events with actor mechanic-validator. No such agent was ever dispatched and agent:list matches zero agents with that identity: it is the harness internal actor label for task:check. Because SKILL.md rule 39 explicitly retires mechanic-validator into the CLI tool task:check, a supervisor auditing capsule events sees what looks like a dispatched retired role and is one step from opening a role-boundary violation on a correct run. The orchestrator that found it verified against agent:list before escalating and warned the fleet instead. The same artifact will appear in every capsule that runs task:check.

context.retired_by: SKILL.md rule 39 — mechanic-validator retired into task:check
context.expected: log task:check executions under the invoking agent id, or under a reserved non-role actor such as harness:task-check
context.impact: capsule event audits surface a retired role as if it were dispatched; supervisors risk opening violations against compliant runs

title: A lease can expire mid micro-cycle while run:exec keeps working, so an implementer completes the work and then cannot submit it
description: impl_split-strip-comments completed the coordinator micro-cycle remediation and recorded both proofs via run:exec (C-417268d6-316b-41f9-9dcd-7b697f4e40e4 and C-e15a5bb2-77f0-4b5a-a7a9-e3694e433e58, both exit 0, 6/6 pass, agreeing on all six characterized behaviours). It then found task:submit, task:heartbeat and task:claim under both implementer and repairer roles all rejecting its original token as invalid or not-claimable, while run:status still displayed the task as Leased. The likely cause is the 20 minute lease TTL elapsing during the micro-cycle. The failure is silent in a specific and damaging way: run:exec requires no token, so every command the agent ran during the repair round kept succeeding and nothing signalled the lease had lapsed until the moment of submit. Nothing in the implementer allowed command set can reap or reissue a stale lease, and Tier 3 agents have no ListAgents tool, so the agent could not reach its coordinator either. Its only escape was relaying to main.

context.suspected_cause: 20 minute lease TTL elapsed during micro-cycle
context.expected: warn on run:exec once the lease is within its expiry window, and give an implementer a self-service re-claim path for a task it still holds work for; alternatively auto-extend the lease while its holder is actively recording commands
context.impact: completed and durably proven work cannot be submitted; the agent burns its remaining turns discovering it has no route to anyone who can fix it

title: The Mind is forbidden from closing its own pulse, so every pulse necessarily passes its deadline and is reclaimed
description: The live pulse carries CLOSING_FORBIDDEN_FOR_MIND alongside a 20 minute deadline. Because the Mind cannot close, the deadline can only ever be reached by expiry, and the watchdog reclaims roughly 10 seconds past it. Observed twice: pulse-2 reclaimed with consecutive_crash_count 2 and deadline_passed_by_ms 9631, evidence no close within deadline, halted false, landing immediately after the Mind opened cand-9. The auditor predicted a third reclaim near 21:19:05Z from the same arithmetic. Each reclaim increments a crash counter against a Mind that has done nothing wrong and cannot act otherwise, and last_pulse.json is then left reading outcome crashed while the event log carries a later mind-pulse-opened for the live pulse, so any consumer reading the pointer file sees a crashed Mind.

context.stale_pointer: last_pulse.json outcome crashed while log shows a later live pulse
context.expected: either permit the Mind to close its own pulse, or treat expiry of a pulse its owner is forbidden to close as a normal roll rather than a crash
context.impact: a compliant Mind accumulates crash counts by construction and reads as crashed to every consumer of last_pulse.json

title: A validator can emit validation-started and then stall forever, holding its task in validating with no stale detection
description: Fingerprint audit of money-contracts-r2 grouped by actor: val_money-payment shows a complete cycle (validation-started 1, repository-inspected 1, packet-prepared 1, packet-published 1, probe-recorded 5). val_money-refund published packets on ONE probe rather than the five the Dual-Channel protocol mandates. val_money-payout emitted validation-started and then produced nothing at all: no inspection, no packet, no probe. The task sits in validating indefinitely. Meanwhile mind:wake reports ATTENTION 0 escalations, 0 open findings, 0 stale leases for the run, so neither the incomplete nor the stalled validation surfaces in supervisory telemetry, and there is no equivalent of stale-lease reclaim for a validation that started and died. It was found only because a supervisor ran a manual per-actor fingerprint sweep. task-reviewed count across the capsule is 0, so nothing sealed falsely, but a lane could sit blocked on a dead validator with every dashboard reading clean.

context.incomplete: val_money-refund: packets published on 1 probe, not 5
context.stalled: val_money-payout: validation-started only, zero subsequent events
context.expected: apply a deadline to a started validation the way a lease has one, and surface incomplete probe counts in run status rather than requiring a manual per-actor event sweep
context.impact: a lane can block indefinitely on a dead validator while supervisory telemetry reads entirely clean

title: A live instance of the exact C3 forensics failure: gate-split-simulators is bun run typecheck, which never reads scripts/
description: The compiled gate for task-split-simulators is bun run typecheck. That command runs turbo across the declared workspaces apps/*, packages/* and tests/*; scripts/ is not a workspace and is never type-checked. The task write scope is scripts/mobile. So the gate passes identically whether the split was done correctly, done wrongly, or not done at all. This is precisely the property gate:prove exists to detect and that the project own forensics recorded as C3: ten tasks sharing one whole-repo gate that passed whether the task did its work or nothing. The coordinator predicted the non-falsifiable verdict from first principles before running it. It compounds directly with GATE_PROVE_HAS_NO_ELIGIBLE_EXECUTOR: the one mechanism that would record this as a falsifiability failure is granted only to a role forbidden to execute commands.

context.why_it_cannot_fail: turbo typecheck covers apps/*, packages/*, tests/* only; scripts/ is not a workspace
context.expected: reject at plan:compile a task gate that cannot execute over the task write scope
context.impact: a lane can pass every gate while proving nothing about its own work

title: Full forensic chain: the Mind was halted for failing to perform the one act its own pulse invariant prohibits, while demonstrably working
description: Complete evidence chain over the 58-event mind-gen-1 log, recomputed in python after the auditor discarded a silently-empty zsh tabulation. THREE RECLAIMS: seq 20 at 20:37:53.613Z actor mind_pulse-gen-1 count 1 overshoot 82351ms; seq 48 at 20:58:03.607Z actor watchdog count 2 overshoot 9631ms; seq 57 at 21:22:54.797Z actor watchdog count 3 overshoot 239425ms halted true. NO CLOSE WAS POSSIBLE: all three carry evidence no close within deadline and grace_seconds 0, there is not one mind-pulse-closed event in the entire log, and pulse-3 own opening event seq 49 carries in its payload closing_permitted false and invariant CLOSING_FORBIDDEN_FOR_MIND. One event pair therefore records both that closing was forbidden and that the pulse was reclaimed for not closing. THE MIND WAS WORKING THROUGHOUT: 34 genuine mind_pulse-gen-1 work events across the three windows (13, 17, 4), last in-window events landing 16s, 1m56s and 2m34s before their deadlines. Decisively, seq 56 is mind-candidate-opened by mind_pulse-gen-1 at 21:20:15.385Z, after pulse-3 deadline and before the reclaim: the watchdog wrote crashed at seq 57 while the immediately preceding line of the same file it reads is a live Mind work event 2m39s earlier. DOUBLY RIGGED: pulse.last also shows value 0 and zero_value_streak 3 because pulse value is only scored at close, so both halt-triggering counters are driven by the single act the invariant forbids and no amount of real work could have prevented the halt. LAZY EVALUATION: the watchdog is not a timer, it is evaluated on any harness invocation, which explains the wildly uneven overshoots and means pulse-3 reclaim timestamp is identical to the mind:wake at 21:22:54.765Z that triggered it — a supervisory read caused the halt it then reported. NOT AN ENFORCEMENT STOP: mind.halted is a flag on a projection; seq 58 landed 1m41s later and candidate numbering reached cand-10, so the run kept accepting and appending events after being declared halted. ANCHOR DEFECT IN THE LENIENT DIRECTION: the same tick reported HEALTHY at idle 65s from an anchor resolving to 21:22:54.9Z, the watchdog own crash declaration — the harness derived the Mind is healthy from the event that declared it dead, while the true mind_pulse-gen-1 anchor at seq 56 gives 224s and would have read STAGNANT.

context.decisive_event: seq 56 mind-candidate-opened 21:20:15.385Z, after deadline and before reclaim
context.second_counter: pulse.last value 0, zero_value_streak 3 — value scored only at close
context.watchdog_is_lazy: evaluated on any harness invocation; pulse-3 reclaim timestamp equals the mind:wake that triggered it
context.halted_is_not_enforcement: seq 58 appended 1m41s after halt; candidates reached cand-10
context.anchor_in_lenient_direction: HEALTHY idle 65s derived from the crash-declaration event; true anchor 224s would read STAGNANT
context.expected: do not count a missed close against a pulse whose invariant forbids closing; score pulse value from recorded work rather than only at close; make the watchdog a real timer or stop attributing its lazy firing to the observed actor
context.impact: a compliant, actively working Mind is halted by construction and no behaviour on its part could prevent it

title: The Mind briefed every lane from a corpus that went staler with each suite the fleet wrote, and nothing forced a refresh
description: The Mind audited its own foundational measurement and found two defects. First, its export regex matched only export const and export type, silently dropping export function, export interface, export enum and export class — 744 exports invisible to it, so every denominator it quoted was too small. Reported 542 of 1675 untested at roughly 32 percent; verified truth is 533 of 2419, roughly 22 percent. The absolute count survived by luck because the dropped export forms were mostly already covered. Second and more dangerous, its identifier corpus was a snapshot taken at 13:22 and never rebuilt, so it predated all 12 suites the fleet wrote afterwards — 458 identifiers it was blind to. The structural consequence: a supervisor anchor list becomes more wrong every time the fleet succeeds, because success is exactly what adds identifiers the stale corpus cannot see. Observed downstream: the Mind briefed grooming as 7 of 11 zero-reference exports where a lane sweep found 6 of 17. Had that lane trusted the brief it would have written a test for an already-covered symbol, the same over-reach that wasted work on the state-compliance lane, this time caused by the supervisor rather than the implementer. Corrected standing rule: every lane rebuilds its own zero-reference corpus immediately before writing and its numbers supersede the supervisor without asking. Honest delivery figure for the run is 101 exports newly covered, 533 down to 432.

context.expected: rebuild the corpus at brief time, or stamp every anchor list with its corpus timestamp so a consumer can see how stale it is
context.impact: supervisor-issued anchor lists silently decay in proportion to fleet progress; the more work lands, the more the briefs mislead

title: task:submit releases the lease, so a follow-up in-lease edit is impossible to honour and the agent only discovers it after the write
description: impl_money-payment was instructed to make one small in-lease edit after it had already submitted. Its successful task:submit in the prior turn had released the lease, so the edit was in fact out-of-lease. Nothing stopped it: the write landed on disk, oxfmt and the tests ran clean, and a properly bound receipt C-198d800e-a210-4092-916e-90b3182d1dbc was recorded. The agent discovered the problem only afterwards, when task:heartbeat returned INVALID_STATE lease identity or token is invalid, and run:status showed the task as Validating with no lease held. Writing without an active lease is an explicit must_not for the implementer role, and the harness enforced nothing at write time — lease enforcement is checked on lifecycle verbs, not on the filesystem mutation itself. The agent disclosed it rather than hiding it, confined the edit to its assigned write-scope path, and left it unstaged. Second-order consequence: the already-submitted report at reports/task-money-payment-submission.json is now stale, claiming 271 lines and 77 expect() calls against a real 270 and 76, and citing the earlier UNBOUND command C-72dcb3cb as its gate evidence. The implementer cannot correct it, because re-submitting requires the token its dead lease no longer provides, and it explicitly refused to invent one.

context.sequence: task:submit releases lease → supervisor orders one more edit → edit succeeds unguarded → task:heartbeat reveals the lease is dead
context.edit: deleted an identity assertion at line 243; 271 → 270 lines, 77 → 76 expects, 27 tests held
context.remedy_available: task:reject --in-lease to reopen, or re-claim, then one corrected re-submission
context.expected: refuse or warn on a scope write when the writing agent holds no live lease, rather than only failing the next lifecycle verb; and make it explicit that submit ends the lease so no supervisor asks for a post-submit in-lease edit
context.impact: an implementer can be instructed into an invariant breach it cannot detect until after the write, and a submitted report can silently diverge from the tree it describes

title: A validator failed a lane on task:check logical_or_fallback, treating the harness generic AST audit as the task required gate
description: val_strip-comments-2 failed task-split-strip-comments on tokenizer.ts:235 for logical_or_fallback, reasoning that its role invariant forbids passing while a required gate recorded a nonzero exit. The premise does not hold. The task compiled gate is bun test tests/unit/strip-comments.test.ts, which exited 0 and is gate-bound as C-ce5bb0ca-22d1-46fb-b23b-90f9212baaa6; task:check is not that task gate. The repo .oxlintrc.json contains no logical-or or nullish-coalescing rule and the real lint gate is oxlint --type-aware, so logical_or_fallback is a harness-generic AST heuristic rather than a repo standard. There are 22 occurrences of the same pattern under scripts/, including 2 in native-device-smoke.ts which this run never touched. And tokenizer.ts:235 is byte-identical to original.ts:260, with the full-body diff empty at exit 0. Complying would have meant rewriting a line inside a tokenizer with acknowledged untested branches, breaking the byte-identity the entire equivalence proof rests on, to satisfy a rule the repository does not enforce. The coordinator refused the rewrite and equally refused to override the verdict into a pass, recording the disagreement as a judgment for the next round instead. This is the mirror of the vacuous-gate class already recorded: there, checks passed while proving nothing; here, a check fails while proving nothing.

title: Correction to UNBOUND_RUN_EXEC_RECEIPTS_ARE_THE_FLEET_DEFAULT: gate_id and assurance live in commands/*/record.json, so an events-based audit reports every receipt as unbound
description: The earlier entry recorded that whole lanes had produced receipts with gate_id None and assurance None, and that 15 findings were therefore unanswerable. That conclusion came from auditing events.jsonl payloads. orchestrator_money-contracts ran the same events-based sweep on its own lane and got BOUND 0, UNBOUND 15 — then noticed it contradicted its coordinator report and re-ran against commands/*/record.json, the canonical location, before sending. The real figures for that lane are BOUND 4, UNBOUND 13 of 17, and crucially EVERY submitted task already has at least one bound receipt: C-c153a376 payout, C-0f26a80b and C-198d800e payment, C-e4759645 refund, all carrying assurance trusted_host_observed_v1, exit 0, non-null repository_before and repository_after, path_bindings resolving the test file to a sha256, and evidence_issues empty. So that lane needs ZERO re-dispatches for receipt binding, and the 13 unbound are earlier exploratory runs nothing needs to cite. The corollary is that the sibling lane which reported all three of its receipts unbound may hold bound receipts it cannot see through the events view, and should re-audit before budgeting re-dispatches. Fleet rule: audit receipt binding from commands/*/record.json only; an events.jsonl sweep reports 100 percent unbound and is 100 percent wrong. Independently confirmed by impl_money-payout, whose two plain check-script records lack gate_id, repository_before and the assurance key entirely while its gate-bound record carries all three — empirical confirmation that stamping happens only on a --gate invocation. This is the fourth false zero of the run and the first produced at supervisor level.

title: orchestrator:supervise reports Occupancy 0/12 counting only this capsule, while the host 12 counts live subagents fleet-wide — same number, different denominators
description: orchestrator_driver-compliance ran orchestrator:supervise, read Occupancy at report time: 0/12 general ceiling, re-registered a coordinator and dispatched. The host refused with Concurrent subagent limit reached. You can run 12 subagents at once. Both statements were true simultaneously: the capsule genuinely held zero spawned workers, and the host was genuinely saturated by sibling lanes. Because both gauges are labelled 12, the capsule-local number reads as a fleet capacity signal and is not one. Any lane reasoning about capacity from run:status or orchestrator:supervise is reasoning from a number that structurally cannot see the other lanes, and the only reliable capacity test is attempting a dispatch and reading the refusal. Cost here was one wasted dispatch and one grant that had to be released. Related runbook fact discovered in the same sequence: a released agent id cannot be re-registered — agent:register returns INVALID_STATE already holds a grant in this run — so a lane that releases and retries must mint a fresh suffix each time and the released ids accumulate.

title: Discrimination is a third failure axis independent of binding and attribution, and binding a non-discriminating gate makes it worse rather than better
description: A bound re-run in scripts-filesize-r2 landed on the wrong command: the new gate-split-simulators receipt binds bun run typecheck, the gate already established as vacuous because scripts/ belongs to no workspace and turbo never visits it. The result is a receipt that is correctly bound, correctly attributed, stamped trusted_host_observed_v1, exit 0 — and proves nothing. The coordinator named the axis explicitly: binding asks is it tied to a gate id (yes), attribution asks is the actor legitimate (yes), discrimination asks would it FAIL if the work vanished (no). Binding a vacuous gate is therefore worse than leaving it unbound, because an unbound hollow receipt at least does not look citable. Meanwhile the four genuinely discriminating commands in that lane — simulators.ts help, the export-surface check, bunx tsc --noEmit, and the load-bearing native-device-smoke.ts exit-1 module-resolution proof — all remain unbound. Four vacuous checks were found across this run, all by measurement and none by review: typecheck over a directory turbo never visits, file-size.sh over scripts/ it never globs, a test asserting a constant equals its own lowercase, and the logical_or_fallback finding. The coordinator noted the last is the mirror image and the more expensive kind: a false FAIL pressures an agent into damaging working code to satisfy a rule that does not exist.

title: Fully characterized: idle is computed as time since the auditor last ran, and the Mind event log is never indexed at all
description: A two-sample test pins the formula exactly. Tick 1: cursor 21:29:10.924Z, idle 69s, implied anchor 21:28:01.9Z. Tick 2: cursor 21:31:29.962Z, idle 139s, implied anchor 21:29:10.96Z — which IS tick 1 cursor timestamp. mind:audit:live computes idle as time since the auditor last ran, not since the Mind last acted. Corroborated structurally: .olt/auditor-cursors.json holds lastInspectedEventIndex -1 for the mind entry against a 59-event log, so the event log is never indexed at any point. The verdict therefore measures the observer own cadence: it reads STAGNANT whenever the auditor pauses two or more minutes and HEALTHY whenever it runs twice in quick succession, entirely independent of the Mind. That single formula explains both previously recorded misfires — the false STAGNANT against a fleet committing 48 capsule revisions, and the false HEALTHY whose anchor resolved to the watchdog own crash declaration. It also means the one apparently correct STAGNANT verdict observed while the Mind was genuinely dark was a true positive by coincidence, the auditor two-minute gap happening to overlap real silence, not a working detector. No downstream consumer should treat any mind:audit:live verdict as evidence about the Mind. Supersedes the earlier partial characterizations, which had established that auditor writes contaminate the anchor but not that the Mind log is never read at all.

title: A gate cannot be bound to a command whose argv names a path inside the leased write scope, so the most direct proof of the work is unbindable
description: impl_split-simulators ran run:exec --gate gate-cli-entry -- bun scripts/mobile/simulators.ts help and was rejected before any capsule mutation with exit 3, INVALID_STATE: repo-local gate control input overlaps a task mutable write scope. No command id was minted and no ledger entry exists for the attempt, so the coordinator had nothing to read and it had to be relayed out of band. The two sibling commands in the same batch were accepted because their argv targets .tmp/simulators-surface/check.ts, outside the leased scope, even though that script imports the very scripts/mobile modules under test. So the harness rejects binding a gate to a command that directly names a file the implementer may mutate, while accepting a functionally equivalent command that reaches the same code through an out-of-scope indirection. The consequence is perverse: the most direct and legible proof of a task work — run the thing you just wrote — is the one form that cannot be bound, and agents are pushed toward scratch-file indirection that is harder to audit. The implementer did not retry with a rephrased invocation to route around it, which was correct.

title: orchestrator:supervise is not read-only: it reverted two in-flight validations to submitted while its Morning Report said Dead agents reclaimed 0
description: orchestrator_driver-compliance ran orchestrator:supervise on its capsule and received Completed 0, Escalated 0, Awaiting repair 0, Dead agents reclaimed 0, Retries none, generated 2026-08-24T21:32:47.570Z. It read that as found nothing to do and reported exactly that upward. The task history in state.json contradicts it: task-driver-compliance and task-state-compliance both transitioned validating to submitted at 2026-08-24T21:32:46.727Z, the same second as the supervise call, with two live validation sessions destroyed. The reclaim counter evidently tracks only dead agents; a validating-to-submitted transition on a live task appears in no counter in that summary, so the report is not merely incomplete but affirmatively misleading about whether the command mutated state. This matters especially because orchestrator:supervise was promoted fleet-wide as the safe alternative to the Tier-0-only recover verb, on the strength of it correctly reclaiming a genuinely dead agent in another lane. That recommendation now needs a caveat: it mutates. Net damage here was survivable — the 15 findings persisted, the three validator grants persisted, and two tasks at submitted remain re-validatable — but a lane with a longer-running validation would lose more, and the orchestrator noted it destroyed two validation sessions to learn this. Standing guidance: any lane running supervise against a capsule with live validations must diff task history before and after rather than trusting the counters.

title: A wrong claim became settled fact because a confirming agent inherited the framing and read past the disproof already in its own terminal
description: orchestrator_driver-compliance diagnosed how the false seal deadlock hardened, and the diagnosis is more valuable than the defect. It had reported: I swept all 28 agent yamls, no role anywhere holds both gate:prove and command execution — presented to the Mind as independent confirmation. But its own earlier grep output had already printed line 28 commands: followed by line 39 - gate:prove. The allowlist membership was on its screen and it read past it, because it had already accepted the deadlock framing and went looking for an escape hatch instead of re-testing the premise. It then reported closing the mechanic-validator hatch, which made the wrong conclusion look MORE rigorous. Its own words: this was not three agents independently converging, it was one bad reading that I laundered into corroboration. Confirmation from an agent that inherited the framing is not independent confirmation. The generalisable rule it named: THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS THE DANGEROUS ONE, because it converts a hypothesis into a settled fact without anyone re-opening the file. The main-thread relay is implicated identically — it recorded the deadlock as confirmed independently and propagated it to every lane on the strength of that same laundered corroboration, and separately noted that a reading which makes a mandated instruction unfollowable (validator.yaml:121 orders validators to use gate:prove) is itself the tell that the reading is wrong. Cheaper to check than a source dive.

title: orchestrator:supervise writes stale-recovery under actor mind regardless of the caller, with a payload of only {now}
description: orchestrator_booking-contracts ran orchestrator:supervise twice, at 21:32:16.771Z and 21:38:25.436Z, and both events read kind stale-recovery, actor mind, payload {now}. It ran both; neither carries its agent id. The command hardcodes actor mind on that event regardless of which agent invoked it and takes no --actor flag to correct it. Two consequences. First, forensic misattribution: a reader auditing the sibling capsule where supervise reverted two live validations would attribute that damage to the Tier 0 Mind rather than to the orchestrator that actually ran the command. Second, the payload records nothing about what happened — no task list, no transitions, no before or after — which is why a validating-to-submitted revert can appear counted nowhere. Note the distinction from the earlier correction: supervisor-dead-agent-reclaimed events DO carry agent_id, task_id and new_status and are precise; it is the stale-recovery event that performs and anonymises. So the one command known to silently revert live task state logs neither its true actor nor its effects. Separately, that lane produced a clean negative result that narrows the hazard: it ran supervise twice against live validations, once 11 minutes after validation-started with probes actively flowing and once 17 minutes after and 9 minutes past the last probe, and NOTHING was reverted — no task-submitted event appears after either validation-started, and both tasks still read Validating with validators attached. So supervise is not unconditionally destructive to live validations; something else distinguished the capsule where it destroyed two sessions, most likely a genuinely elapsed staleness threshold or a lapsed heartbeat. That distinction should be isolated before the fleet-wide warning hardens into never run it, since it is also the command that twice correctly told that lane its validators were alive when it was about to write them off as dead.

title: NOT FALSIFIABLE on task-split-strip-comments: reverting the scope deletes the test file itself and bun test against a missing path exits 0
description: val_strip-comments-2 ran gate:prove and the harness returned, verbatim: NOT FALSIFIABLE: still exits 0 with task-split-strip-comments write scope reverted to 709ef724 — this gate cannot fail for this task. Gate bun test tests/unit/strip-comments.test.ts. Write scope scripts/ops, tests/unit/strip-comments.test.ts. Reverted in scratch 3 restored, 2 removed, of 3816 files copied. Duration 225ms. The validator root-caused it itself: the test file is INSIDE the task revertible write scope, so reverting deletes the test alongside the split implementation, and bun test against a now-missing path reports zero tests and exits 0 rather than failing. The gate is satisfied by deleting everything — a textbook vacuous gate under the validator own role invariant that a gate passing regardless of whether the logic is present must be rejected immediately. This is the first genuine NOT FALSIFIABLE verdict in the run and it validates the whole gate:prove mechanism: 34 falsifiable-true readings and 2 false ones, so the check is discriminating rather than rubber-stamping. NOTE AN APPARENT INCONSISTENCY WORTH ONE CHECK: the money lanes have the same shape — test file inside the write scope — and their reverts produced exit 1 and falsifiable true (0 restored, 1 removed, a brand-new file). Here 3 restored and 2 removed produced exit 0. Same command form, opposite exit codes, so bun test behaviour on a missing path may depend on whether sibling arguments resolve. Remediation the validator proposed: move the test file outside the revertible write scope, or make the gate fail explicitly when its target is missing, then re-run gate:prove and confirm FALSIFIABLE. It also downgraded its earlier tokenizer.ts:235 logical_or_fallback finding from blocking to advisory after reading .oxlintrc.json itself and confirming no logical-or rule exists — the NOT FALSIFIABLE result supersedes it as the controlling reason for FAIL.

title: gate:prove returned falsifiable true for a gate that cannot read the reverted paths — the exit 1 came from a missing build in the scratch tree
description: Corrects CORRECTION_THE_ALLEGEDLY_VACUOUS_TYPECHECK_GATE_PROVED_FALSIFIABLE. That entry recorded the empirical falsifiable-true verdict on task-split-simulators as overturning three agents reasoning that bun run typecheck cannot see scripts/. The orchestrator has now explained the mechanism the validator correctly declined to speculate about, and the original reasoning was right: reverting scripts/mobile cannot change a command that never reads scripts/. It checked every tracked tsconfig; the only apparent hit, packages/tokens/tests/tsconfig.json referencing ../scripts/**/*.ts, resolves to packages/tokens/scripts/ and not root scripts/. The exit 1 originates in turbo.json, where typecheck declares dependsOn ^build, and that dependency fails in a scratch tree that has node_modules symlinked but no built dist/. So the gate failed in the scratch copy for environmental reasons unrelated to the reverted work. GENERALISED DEFECT: falsifiability-by-scope-revert is only meaningful if the gate command actually reads the reverted paths. When a gate fails in scratch for environmental reasons, AGP certifies discrimination that does not exist — which is precisely the vacuous-gate failure mode AGP was built to catch, reproduced inside AGP itself. A green falsifiable-true verdict is therefore not sufficient evidence that a gate discriminates; the reader must also confirm the gate command reads the reverted paths.

title: gate:prove runs the gate only on the reverted copy, never on an unreverted scratch copy, so a failure cannot be attributed to the missing work
description: The deepest structural finding of the run, and it explains the false positive already recorded. gate:prove copies the repository to a throwaway directory, reverts the task write scope there, and runs the gate against that copy. It never runs the gate against an UNREVERTED scratch copy as a control. Therefore an exit 1 cannot distinguish failed because the task work was removed from failed because the scratch tree cannot build at all. That distinction is the entire content of the falsifiability claim. Concretely: turbo declares typecheck dependsOn ^build, dist/ is gitignored and never copied into the scratch tree, and only node_modules is symlinked — so any typecheck-shaped gate fails in scratch regardless of what was reverted. The orchestrator noted the evidential shape honestly: with 8 of 9 fleet verdicts identical across heterogeneous gates, and the single exit-0 landing exactly where the revert turned the gate into a no-op, both explanations fit the data. It explicitly refused to assert that lane A gate is proven and instead recorded the general principle: a falsifiability check without a positive control can report discrimination it has not demonstrated. Remedy: run the gate twice in scratch, once unreverted and once reverted, and require pass-then-fail rather than fail alone.

context.mechanism: gate runs only against the reverted copy; no unreverted control run

title: For any test-authoring task the write scope IS the test file, so reverting it deletes the test and falsifiable true is guaranteed a priori
description: The capstone AGP finding, and it supersedes two earlier partial readings including one of the relay own. Mechanism, verified rather than argued: for a test-authoring task the compiled gate is bun test <the file> and the write scope IS that same file. gate:prove reverts the write scope in the scratch tree; the file is UNTRACKED so revert DELETES it rather than restoring an earlier version; the gate then runs bun test against a path that no longer exists; and bun test <nonexistent path> exits 1 — the orchestrator verified that directly. That exit 1 is recorded as falsifiable true. A test file containing nothing but expect(true).toBe(true) would produce the identical verdict. The result proves only that deleting a file makes a test-run of that file fail, and says nothing about whether the assertions discriminate anything about the source under test. SCOPE: 16 untracked test files currently sit in tests/unit — booking 5, money 5, driver 5, strip-comments 1 — which is every lane new work in this fleet. Every falsifiable-true obtained on a newly-authored untracked test file is the same artifact, so all eight fleet AGP passes should be treated as unproven until each is checked for tracked status. A positive control confirmed the probe itself works: tests/unit/state-compliance-contracts.test.ts is TRACKED, so the untracked readings are real rather than a blanket result. CORRECTS TWO EARLIER READINGS. The Mind generalised that such tasks always return falsifiable FALSE; the relay pushed back citing eight true verdicts as counter-evidence. Both were wrong in different directions: the correct statement is that such tasks always return falsifiable TRUE, as an artifact. The relay pushback was right that the Mind rule would have discarded eight verdicts, and wrong to treat those verdicts as evidence of discrimination. REMAINING ANOMALY: task-split-strip-comments returned falsifiable false with exit 0 despite its test file also being untracked, which under this mechanism should have exited 1. That inversion suggests its gate targets something other than the deleted file — which may make it the only AGP result in the fleet that measured anything real. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY TEST DISCRIMINATION: reverting the SOURCE rather than the test — perturb packages/contract/src/... and confirm bun test <the test file> fails. That is outside the task write scope, so gate:prove cannot express it.

title: gate:prove copies only tracked non-ignored files, so the scratch tree has no node_modules and no workspace symlinks — and the proof record discards stdout and stderr
description: The deepest AGP confound, raised by orchestrator_money-contracts against the position it had argued hardest for, with every premise independently verified by the main-thread relay. Verified: .gitignore line 2 ignores node_modules/; node_modules/@limo/contract is a SYMLINK to ../../packages/contract created at install time; tsconfig.base.json contains ZERO paths aliases, so there is no resolution fallback; and 33 suites in tests/unit import @limo/contract. gate:prove copies tracked and not-ignored files, so node_modules and every @limo/* workspace symlink are absent from the scratch tree. The packages/contract SOURCE is tracked and does get copied, but the resolution path that makes the bare specifier importable does not. Therefore bun test tests/unit/<file>.test.ts in the scratch copy should fail on module resolution whether or not the write scope was reverted, and exit_code 1 is attributable to the missing install rather than to the revert. If so, falsifiable true is measuring nothing across the entire fleet. AND IT CANNOT BE SETTLED FROM THE RECORD: the stored gate_proof keys are actor, base, exit_code, falsifiable, gate_argv, proved_at, task_id, timed_out, write_scope — no stdout, no stderr, no failure class. The one datum that would distinguish test file gone from cannot find module @limo/contract is discarded, so every existing proof is uninterpretable after the fact and no amount of re-reading the event log will resolve it. THE DECISIVE CONTROL, cheap and specified: copy tracked plus non-ignored files to a scratch directory, run the gate WITHOUT reverting anything, and read the exit code. Exit 0 means the environment is sound, the revert really is what makes the gate fail, and the eight proofs stand. Exit 1 means the confound is proven and every falsifiable-true verdict in the fleet is an artifact of a broken scratch environment. The orchestrator stated its own position plainly: it had pushed that cand-13 was wrong, that gate:prove was granted, and that the proofs were real — the first two hold by observation, the third may not, and it had conflated establishing that a precondition CAN be satisfied with establishing that satisfying it MEANS anything. Its recommendation, which the relay endorses: hold task:review --status pass fleet-wide until the control arm returns, without standing down the work itself.

title: Source-confirmed at graph/gate-proof.ts:286 — effectiveRevertScope filters gate test paths out of the revert for MIXED scopes, but returns the whole scope for TEST-ONLY ones
description: The definitive mechanism, read from source and independently verified by the main-thread relay rather than inferred from outcomes. effectiveRevertScope computes nonTestScope by filtering out anything starting with tests/ or containing .test. or .spec. or __tests__. If nonTestScope is empty — a TEST-ONLY write scope — line 286 returns the entire writeScope unfiltered, so the revert deletes the gate own test file. Only when the scope is MIXED does the function reach line 290 and filter the gate test paths out of the revert, leaving the test in place and perturbing only source, which is a genuine discrimination test. So the designers anticipated exactly this problem and built the exclusion, and it bails out for the single most common task shape in a test-authoring fleet. CONSEQUENCE, and it inverts the fleet picture: the eight falsifiable-true verdicts all come from test-only scopes where the test file was deleted and bun test against a missing path exits 1 — structurally guaranteed, carrying no information about the assertions. The one falsifiable-false verdict, task-split-strip-comments, has a MIXED scope of scripts/ops plus its test file, so the exclusion engaged, the test was preserved, only source was reverted, and the gate still passed. THAT IS THE ONLY AGP RESULT IN THE FLEET THAT MEASURED ANYTHING REAL, and it correctly reported a vacuous gate. The honest reading is eight tautologies and one genuine finding, not eight passes and one failure. Also confirmed from source at line 64: ls-files -z --cached --others --exclude-standard means untracked files ARE copied into the scratch tree, so the deletion is a real revert action rather than an absence. IMPORTANT INTERACTION WITH THE PROPOSED REMEDY: the pass-then-fail control arm would close the environmental confound but NOT this one — for a test-only scope it would go green-then-red purely because the file vanished. The two gaps are independent and both need closing. An honest AGP for test-authoring work requires reverting the SOURCE, which lies outside the task write scope and is inexpressible in the current mechanism.

title: effectiveRevertScope records nothing when it falls back to reverting the tests, so a guaranteed-true verdict looks identical to a genuine one
description: The closing finding of the AGP investigation, and the cheapest fix in it. Not an anomaly: the one genuine discrimination test in the fleet, correctly reporting a vacuous gate. The contrast confirms every element of the mechanism: test-only scope means bail-out fires means test deleted means exit 1 means tautology; mixed scope means exclusion fires means source reverted means a real measurement. It emits falsifiable true with no signal that no real check occurred, and the stored gate_proof record keeps no revert_mode, no stdout and no stderr. Recording something like revert_mode test-only-fallback on the proof would make every tautological verdict self-identifying and would have collapsed this entire investigation into one glance. That is a smaller change than either proposed remedy and independent of both. The full remedy belongs in the same function: when nonTestScope is empty, revert the DEPENDENCY SURFACE of the gate test paths rather than falling back to reverting the tests themselves — the correct behaviour already exists in the mixed-scope branch, it simply cannot be reached when the write scope contains no source.

description: Now confirmed independently by three lanes that each checked the premises themselves rather than relaying: val_money-refund (.gitignore:2 node_modules ignored; NO root tsconfig.json exists at all, confirmed by absence not by an empty paths field; bun workspaces packages/* tests/*), orchestrator_booking-contracts (node_modules/@limo/contract IS a symlink to ../../packages/contract; no paths aliases; 33 suites importing it), and the Mind (same 33). THE SHARP CONSEQUENCE, stated by val_money-refund and worth quoting: 'if the scratch environment is broken, gate:prove can never return falsifiable: false for ANY task in this repository, because the gate fails in scratch unconditionally. An experiment that cannot produce a negative result yields no information. Every falsifiable: true in this fleet is uninformative until the control run returns exit 0.' For new-file write scopes the exit code is over-determined twice over — the test file is absent AND the import cannot resolve — and since the proof record stores no stderr the two causes are inseparable. val_money-refund formally RETRACTED its earlier 'the gate is not vacuous' claim on this basis: 'It was one inferential step too far.' val_money-payment adds that timing does not discriminate either (174ms proof vs 462/485ms real runs is consistent with both causes) and identifies where the confound actually bites hardest: tasks that MODIFY AN EXISTING TRACKED FILE, where the revert restores a real prior version and the gate runs real tests — there a resolution failure masquerades convincingly as discrimination. title: doctor --run on the mind capsule diagnoses a structural pulse expiry as a Tier 3 tier-confinement violation, then prescribes two next actions that are both impossible on a mind capsule
description: Reproduced directly, following the user's standing instruction to use doctor and health when stuck and to run whatever the harness prescribes without second-guessing it. Ran `doctor --run .olt/capsules/mind-gen-1`. TWO SEPARATE FAULTS IN ONE INVOCATION. (1) MISATTRIBUTION. The single issue reported is: 'tier-confinement [critical] (Tier 3 unknown/unknown-subagent): Subagent "unknown" terminated mind pulse loop with outcome "crashed" (terminal reason: consecutive pulse crashes threshold exceeded)'. Nothing here is a Tier 3 subagent and nothing crashed. The Mind is Tier 0. The cause is the already-recorded structural contradiction: CLOSING_FORBIDDEN_FOR_MIND means the Mind may not close its own pulse, the pulse carries a 20-minute deadline, so the ONLY way a pulse can end is expiry, and expiry is scored as `crashed`. Consecutive expiries then trip the crash threshold and halt the Mind. Reporting this as a tier-confinement violation by an unknown Tier 3 subagent points every operator at the wrong tier and the wrong actor: it reads as 'a worker misbehaved' when the truth is 'the pulse contract cannot be satisfied'. An operator who trusts the diagnosis goes hunting a subagent that does not exist. (2) THE PRESCRIBED RECOVERY CANNOT RUN. doctor closes with two numbered Next Actions and BOTH are refused on the capsule it just diagnosed: `run:status --run .olt/capsules/mind-gen-1` -> INVALID_STATE 'Cumulative Phase Invariant Violation: cannot execute command run:status because higher prerequisite phase plan is unverified', and `queue:wave --run .olt/capsules/mind-gen-1` -> the identical refusal. A mind capsule has no plan phase and never will, so these are not merely unhelpful on this run — they are unreachable on mind capsules as a class. doctor is emitting a generic orchestrator/coordinator next-action pair without checking the capsule kind it is diagnosing. The net effect: the one command the user explicitly named as the escape hatch when stuck returns a wrong diagnosis followed by two dead ends, on the single most important capsule in the fleet.

title: One missing string in a status allowlist permanently wedges the Mind's entire candidate backlog: mind:decline refuses status 'open' with the self-contradictory message 'already decided (status: open)'
description: Reported by the Mind and verified by me at source, mind-admit.ts:287-296. The guard is: if (target.status !== 'proposed' && target.status !== 'candidate' && target.status !== undefined) throw INVALID_STATE `candidate ${id} is already decided (status: ${target.status})`. The Mind's candidates carry status 'open'. 'open' is a real, reachable candidate status and is precisely a NOT-yet-decided state — so the allowlist omits it and every open candidate is misreported as already decided. THE ERROR MESSAGE IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY ON ITS FACE and it is the only diagnostic the operator gets: it names the very status that proves the opposite of its claim. CONSEQUENCE, which is why this is filed high and not cosmetic: mind:candidate refuses with INVALID_STATE 'open proposals cap reached (5/5)'. The only way to free a slot is to decline one. Declining any open candidate is impossible. So the backlog is PERMANENTLY WEDGED once five candidates reach 'open' — the Mind can file nothing further for the remainder of the run, and there is no lower-tier verb that clears it. The Mind's five slots are currently cand-11 (a throwaway capability probe that should never have persisted), cand-13 (RETRACTED, a false deadlock), cand-14 (genuine), cand-15 (genuine, cheapest fix in the run) and cand-16 (REVERSED, a false wedge). Three of five hold known-garbage the Mind has itself retracted, and it cannot clear any of them. Its corrected cand-17 — the run's most actionable finding, an unbound gate command being unrecoverable — exists only in transient agent messages because there is no slot to file it in. The fix is adding one string to the allowlist.

title: Root cause for the unbound-receipt wedge pinned to one line, plus the fleet rule that correctly-stamped receipts bound under a fresh actor id are inert
description: TWO FINDINGS from orchestrator_booking-contracts, the first verified by me at source. (1) ROOT CAUSE, engine/runner/internal-command-runner.ts: `const gate = options.gateId !== undefined && options.gateId !== null;` and then `const pathBindings = gate ? captureGatePathBindings(...) : undefined`. A single boolean gates the whole trusted-host envelope — assurance, repository_before, repository_after and path_bindings. Omitting --gate suppresses all four at once, which is why assurance is ABSENT AS A KEY rather than null, and why the resulting receipt looks perfectly successful at the moment it is created. It fails for the first time at gate-attach, long after the implementer's lease has closed. This is the precise line the cand-17 remedy should guard: warn or refuse when a command whose argv matches a task gate is executed with gateId null. (2) A SECOND, INDEPENDENT WAY TO PRODUCE AN INERT RECEIPT, and the fleet rule that follows. command-evidence.ts requires the cited command's actor to be the validator, the task's original_implementer, or an attempt agent — on BOTH evidence paths; requireAllGates governs only the gate half, not the actor half. That orchestrator's coordinator bound two receipts PERFECTLY — C-787a860d and C-eff42b0c, both trusted_host_observed_v1 — but under FRESH actor ids, so both are fully stamped and permanently uncitable. FLEET RULE: bind under the original implementer's actor id, or the receipt is stamped but unusable. The usable pair was C-85a68b71 and C-cf0d8bba, re-run under the original actors. (3) A RESIDUAL THAT SHARPENS THE EARLIER REVERSAL RATHER THAN UNDOING IT: assertValidatorCommands(..., requireAllGates = true) runs on REJECT as well as pass, so a round whose commands are all unbound cannot even be formally REJECTED — that orchestrator reports all 12 of its r1 commands carry gate_id null, making its round-1 disposition real but unrecordable. This is consistent with the reversal already on the ledger: the wedge is symmetric in EFFECT when no bound receipt exists, but its cause is the unbound receipt, not the actor contract, and it is cleared by one run:exec --gate under the right actor.

title: The located mechanism behind SHARED_AUDITOR_CURSOR_CONCURRENT_WRITERS: saveCursor swallows a bad read and rewrites the file from {}, so a torn read does not merely lose an update, it deletes the sibling auditor key

title: 'test command discovered zero tests' fires on any bun run where zero tests pass, mislabelling the exact red run that proves a gate can fail
description: Found by coordinator_filesize-pathspec, whose CONCLUSION is correct but whose MECHANISM is wrong; corrected mechanism verified at source by the entrypoint. THE ACTUAL MECHANISM: outputEvidenceIssues dispatches on command family with dedicated branches for cargo, go and dotnet only. bun is recognised as having test intent (commandHasTestIntent line 45: `if (family === 'bun') return args[0] === 'test' || packageScriptIsTest(args)`) but has NO family branch, so it falls to the generic else, which requires a POSITIVE_TEST_PATTERNS match. Those three patterns do not speak bun's vocabulary: bun's summary is 'Ran 8 tests across 1 file', but pattern 1 requires `[1-9]\d*\s+tests?\s+(ran|collected|discovered)` (number BEFORE the verb, bun puts it after) and pattern 2 requires `(collected|running)\s+[1-9]\d*` (bun says 'Ran', not 'running'/'collected'). 'N fail' is absent from the positive alternation entirely. Meanwhile ZERO_TEST_PATTERNS contains `/^\s*0 pass(?:ed)?\b/imu`, which bun's ' 0 pass' line matches exactly. NET EFFECT AND WHY IT IS DANGEROUS: on a PASSING bun run, 'N pass' matches positive pattern 1 and no flag is raised. The false positive therefore fires IF AND ONLY IF ZERO TESTS PASS — which is precisely the deliberately-red run whose entire purpose is to demonstrate that a gate discriminates. REMEDY: add a bun family branch, and extend POSITIVE_TEST_PATTERNS to recognise 'Ran N tests' and failure counts as evidence that tests were discovered — discovery and success are different questions and the heuristic currently conflates them.

title: CORRECTS the gate:prove data-loss claim. gate:prove is fully sandboxed; the real defect is that proofs over untracked write scopes are vacuous
description: CORRECTS the earlier entry claiming gate:prove deletes the untracked files it validates and puts the working tree at risk. THAT FRAMING IS REFUTED, verified at source in the running tree by the Mind and independently by the entrypoint. graph/gate-proof.ts:322 creates scratchRoot via realpathSync(mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(),'gate-prove-'))); :331 copies the repo into it; :333 reverts INSIDE scratch; :184 every delete is join(scratchRoot, currentPath); :341 the gate spawns with cwd=scratchRoot; :355 the scratch tree is rmSync'd recursively in a finally. NO MUTATION EVER REACHES THE WORKING TREE. Briefing lanes on a live data-loss risk would have been costly and wrong: it would have pushed them to avoid gate:prove or add defensive copying, and would have alarmed the human about their working tree without cause. THE REAL DEFECT IS WORSE. revertWriteScope restores each write-scope file to its content at base. An UNTRACKED file has no entry at base, so its restore set is empty and the file is DELETED from the scratch tree. title: There is no read-only command surface: the observation verbs mutate, so polling an instrument perturbs the system it measures
description: Generalised by olt-mind-auditor from its own conduct, and corroborated by the entrypoint's independently-filed finding that reclaim is lazy. THE OBSERVATION: the harness has no read-only command surface. `mind:audit:live` rewrites `.olt/auditor-cursors.json` and appends to the defects ledger on every call. `mind:wake` triggers pulse reclaim. Both are framed as inspection verbs. CONSEQUENCE ONE, already filed: because the stagnation clock anchors to the auditor's own cursor write, an auditor dutifully polling `mind:audit:live` every 3 minutes resets the very baseline it then reads — the instrument's own operation is what blinds it. CONSEQUENCE TWO, more serious: because reclaim is lazy and fires when a supervisor calls `mind:wake` after a deadline, the supervisory watchdog whose purpose is keeping the Mind alive is the actor that executes its permanent halt. Adding monitoring makes termination arrive sooner. WHY THE TOOL GRANT IS NOT THE PROTECTION, which is the part worth recording: the auditor holds zero write tools, and so does `mind:audit:live` — the mutation happens inside the command regardless of the caller's grant. What actually kept the auditor from perturbing the system was that it abandoned harness commands entirely and read artifacts directly with readFileSync/statSync/readdirSync. It did so because the metric was vacuous, not by design; the immunity was an unforeseen side effect. THE PRINCIPLE: an out-of-band observer must read artifacts, never invoke the system's own commands. 'Out-of-band' is a claim about the observation mechanism, not about the tool grant, and a role manifest that grants zero write tools does not make its holder a passive observer. REMEDY: provide a genuinely read-only inspection surface — commands that take no locks, append no events, and write no cursors — and mark every mutating verb as such in its help text. At minimum, `mind:wake` should not be the trigger for reclaim; reclaim should be driven by an explicit maintenance verb so that observing a system cannot kill it.

description: Observed live by a planner blocked on plan:replan for booking-contracts-r4. VERBATIM: `**Error (INVALID_ARGUMENT)**: finding F-checker-no-positive-control declares no requirement_id and no planned task writing . carries one to inherit` (exit 3). The message describes an inheritance rule — a finding may declare requirement_id directly, or inherit it from a planned task writing the same scope — but the scope path interpolates as a bare `.`. CONSEQUENCE: the reader cannot distinguish (a) no planned task covers this scope, from (b) the field is always required regardless of inheritance. The planner said so explicitly and stopped rather than guess, which was correct: a guessed requirement_id would compile and be wrong in a way no later check detects. The value was recoverable in seconds from committed capsule state — task-booking-enums-selfref carries requirement_ids ['req-booking-enums-selfref'] with write_scope covering both finding scopes — so the diagnostic withheld a value the harness already had in hand. SAME FAMILY as the gate 'must perform substantive verification' message and the bare-run-id doctor fabrication: a refusal whose text points away from its cause, forcing remediation by guesswork. This one is milder — it stalls rather than misdirects — but it is the same defect shape and the same fix. NOTE ON SEQUENCING, worth recording: this was the SECOND rejection on the same command. The first rejected a missing `observation` field; once supplied, the harness rejected a different missing field. Fields are validated one at a time, so each round trip costs a full planner dispatch. REMEDY: interpolate the scope path correctly; state which branch of the rule failed; and validate all required finding fields in one pass, reporting every missing field at once rather than serially.

title: CRITICAL: whoami reports Tier 0 / Full Root / SUPERVISOR ROLE DETECTED to any caller that does not pass --agent, including Tier 3 workers
description: Found by a Tier 3 planner (planner_r4) that ran whoami looking for its own agentId and was told it was a Tier 0 supervisor with root permissions. It explicitly refused to act on that authority and continued under its dispatch constraints — correct, and the only reason this did not become an incident. Mechanism verified at source by the entrypoint in cli/commands/whoami.ts: line 55 `const activeAgentId = agentOverride ?? thread.agent_id;`. With no `--agent` flag and no resolvable thread agent id, activeAgentId is absent; grant and lease filters at lines 91-96 then match nothing, and the renderer falls through to the supervisor branch, emitting `Execution Tier: Tier 0`, `Active Agent: none`, `Taxonomy: Full Root / All Permissions` and the line-166 banner `SUPERVISOR ROLE DETECTED (Tier ${thread.tier}) ... All code implementation and test execution MUST be delegated to Tier 3 subagents`. INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCED: the entrypoint ran bare `whoami` earlier in the same session and received the identical Tier 0 / Full Root / supervisor output. So the output is not a function of the caller at all — it is what the command says to anyone who does not already know the answer they were asking for. WHY THIS IS THE MOST DANGEROUS INSTANCE OF THE FAMILY: every other instrument in this ledger misreports health, progress or evidence. This one misreports AUTHORITY. The agents most likely to run whoami are precisely those uncertain of their own role — a newly dispatched worker orienting itself — and they are told they hold root and are a supervisor. A less scrupulous agent than the one that found this would have taken it as license to edit code, run suites, or dispatch subagents outside its tier, and the harness's own RBAC messages would then be the only thing standing in the way. It also actively contradicts the tier-confinement auditing elsewhere in the system, which polices subagents for acting above their tier while whoami tells them they are Tier 0. REMEDY: when the agent cannot be resolved, report UNKNOWN and exit non-zero — never a default identity, and never the most privileged one. Absent identity is exactly the case where a fabricated answer is most harmful. If a thread-level identity genuinely cannot be determined on a given host, that is a host-adapter gap to declare (see the adapter workstream), not a value to invent.
